claim: 75% of planarian protein-coding genes are multiexonic.
source: Most planarian protein-coding genes (75%) are multiexonic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from genome annotation analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Planarian intron length displays a sharp bimodal distribution with most introns centered on 57 bp and another subset ranging between 1 and 10 Kbps.
source: Intron length displays a sharp bimodal distribution: whereas most introns are relatively small, with lengths centred on 57 bp, another subset ranges between 1 and 10 Kbps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of intron lengths shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 12,276 alternative splicing events were identified in planarians.
source: These approaches yielded 12,276 AS events, the majority of which (56.2%) corresponded to alternatively retained introns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: 56.2% of alternative splicing events in planarians correspond to alternatively retained introns.
source: These approaches yielded 12,276 AS events, the majority of which (56.2%) corresponded to alternatively retained introns (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: 2529 alternative exons that can be either fully included or skipped from mRNAs were identified in planarians.
source: We also identified 2529 alternative exons that can be either fully included or skipped from the mRNAs, including single and multi-cassette events, as well as 262 microexons (exons of length ≤27 nucleotides (nt) (Irimia et al., 2014), 72 of which had length ≤15 nt) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of RNA-Seq data using vast-tools pipeline.

claim: 262 microexons (exons of length ≤27 nucleotides) were identified in planarians, 72 of which had length ≤15 nt.
source: We also identified 2529 alternative exons that can be either fully included or skipped from the mRNAs, including single and multi-cassette events, as well as 262 microexons (exons of length ≤27 nucleotides (nt) (Irimia et al., 2014), 72 of which had length ≤15 nt) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: 246 alternative splicing events show increased alternative sequence inclusion levels in neoblasts compared to differentiated cells.
source: By comparing neoblasts versus differentiated cells and whole worms depleted of neoblasts (methods), we identified 246 and 256 AS events with increased and decreased alternative sequence inclusion levels in neoblasts, respectively (X1-included and X1-excluded, together referred to as 'neoblast-differential'; Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNA-Seq analysis between FACS-isolated cell populations.

claim: 256 alternative splicing events show decreased alternative sequence inclusion levels in neoblasts compared to differentiated cells.
source: By comparing neoblasts versus differentiated cells and whole worms depleted of neoblasts (methods), we identified 246 and 256 AS events with increased and decreased alternative sequence inclusion levels in neoblasts, respectively (X1-included and X1-excluded, together referred to as 'neoblast-differential'; Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative RNA-Seq analysis between FACS-isolated cell populations.

claim: RT-PCRs confirmed all 22 tested neoblast-differential exons.
source: RT-PCRs using primers (Supplementary file 1) flanking alternative exon sequences confirmed all (22/22) tested neoblast-differential exons and showed a high correlation between RT-PCR and RNA-Seq inclusion level estimates (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; R2 = 0.92, n = 88).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation using RT-PCR.

claim: There is a high correlation (R2 = 0.92) between RT-PCR and RNA-Seq inclusion level estimates for neoblast-differential exons.
source: RT-PCRs using primers (Supplementary file 1) flanking alternative exon sequences confirmed all (22/22) tested neoblast-differential exons and showed a high correlation between RT-PCR and RNA-Seq inclusion level estimates (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; R2 = 0.92, n = 88).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RT-PCR and RNA-Seq data.

claim: 64 microexons were differentially regulated between X1 and Xins fractions.
source: Among these cassette exons, we detected 64 microexons that were differentially regulated between X1 and Xins fractions, the majority of which (82.8%) were more included in differentiated cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-isolated cell populations.

claim: 82.8% of differentially regulated microexons were more included in differentiated cells.
source: Among these cassette exons, we detected 64 microexons that were differentially regulated between X1 and Xins fractions, the majority of which (82.8%) were more included in differentiated cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-isolated cell populations.

claim: Vertebrate microexons display enrichment in neural and muscle tissues compared to ESCs.
source: Consistent with this bias towards differentiated cells, vertebrate microexons have been recently shown to display enrichment in neural and muscle tissues compared to ESCs (Irimia et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Irimia et al., 2014.

claim: 68.5% of neoblast-differential exons overlapped protein-coding regions and conserved the reading frame.
source: The majority of neoblast-differential exons (68.5%) overlapped protein-coding regions and conserved the reading frame; therefore, they were predicted to generate distinct protein isoforms in neoblasts and differentiated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of alternative exon sequences.

claim: Neoblast-differential exons are predicted to generate distinct protein isoforms in neoblasts and differentiated cells.
source: The majority of neoblast-differential exons (68.5%) overlapped protein-coding regions and conserved the reading frame; therefore, they were predicted to generate distinct protein isoforms in neoblasts and differentiated cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that these exons overlap coding regions and conserve reading frames.

claim: Genes with neoblast-differential exons are significantly enriched in cytoskeleton and cell signalling functions.
source: This set of AS events were significantly enriched in genes involved in cytoskeleton and cell signalling functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), gene ontology categories that were also enriched among ESC-differential alternatively spliced genes in mammals (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Cytoskeleton and cell signalling gene ontology categories are enriched among ESC-differential alternatively spliced genes in mammals.
source: This set of AS events were significantly enriched in genes involved in cytoskeleton and cell signalling functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), gene ontology categories that were also enriched among ESC-differential alternatively spliced genes in mammals (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Han et al., 2013.

claim: Neoblast-differential exons significantly more often overlapped disordered regions of proteins compared to general alternatively spliced and constitutive exons.
source: Interestingly, neoblast-differential exons significantly more often overlapped disordered regions of proteins and avoided structured domains compared to general alternatively spliced and constitutive exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D; p ≤ 4.7 × 10−5 for all comparisons, 3-way Fisher test and proportion tests, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis using Disopred2 for disorder prediction.

claim: Neoblast-differential exons avoided structured domains compared to general alternatively spliced and constitutive exons.
source: Interestingly, neoblast-differential exons significantly more often overlapped disordered regions of proteins and avoided structured domains compared to general alternatively spliced and constitutive exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D; p ≤ 4.7 × 10−5 for all comparisons, 3-way Fisher test and proportion tests, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis using PFAM domain annotation.

claim: Tissue-specific exons in mammals overlap disordered regions of proteins.
source: A similar pattern was described for tissue-specific exons in mammals (Buljan et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2012), suggesting that neoblast-differential exons may also contribute to modulate protein-protein interactions in planarian cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Buljan et al., 2012 and Ellis et al., 2012.

claim: Neoblast-differential exons may contribute to modulate protein-protein interactions in planarian cells.
source: A similar pattern was described for tissue-specific exons in mammals (Buljan et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2012), suggesting that neoblast-differential exons may also contribute to modulate protein-protein interactions in planarian cells.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with mammalian tissue-specific exons.

claim: 107 intron retention events were differentially enriched in X1 fractions compared to 41 in Xins.
source: Notably, 107 IR events were differentially enriched in X1 fractions compared to only 41 in Xins (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-isolated cell populations.

claim: RT-PCRs confirmed all 11 tested X1-included introns.
source: RT-PCRs confirmed all (11/11) tested X1-included introns compared to half (2/4) of X1-excluded (Figures 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; R2 = 0.68, n = 56, for all neoblast-differential introns tested).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation using RT-PCR.

claim: RT-PCRs confirmed half (2/4) of X1-excluded introns.
source: RT-PCRs confirmed all (11/11) tested X1-included introns compared to half (2/4) of X1-excluded (Figures 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; R2 = 0.68, n = 56, for all neoblast-differential introns tested).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation using RT-PCR.

claim: X1-included introns were usually longer than other intron types (P = 7.1 × 10−10).
source: X1-included introns were usually longer than other intron types (Figure 2B, P = 7.1 × 10−10, Wilcoxon Sum Rank test), and belonged to genes that were more highly expressed in differentiated cells than in neoblasts and their progeny (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of intron length distributions.

claim: X1-included introns belonged to genes that were more highly expressed in differentiated cells than in neoblasts and their progeny.
source: X1-included introns were usually longer than other intron types (Figure 2B, P = 7.1 × 10−10, Wilcoxon Sum Rank test), and belonged to genes that were more highly expressed in differentiated cells than in neoblasts and their progeny (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis using cRPKM metric.

claim: Nearly all X1-included IR events were predicted to disrupt the reading frame specifically in neoblasts.
source: Importantly, in contrast to cassette exon events, which were predicted to generate different protein isoforms in neoblast and differentiated cells, nearly all X1-included IR events were predicted to disrupt the reading frame specifically in neoblasts (Figure 2E; p<2.2 × 10−16, chi-squared test).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of open reading frames.

claim: X1-included introns preferentially affected genes significantly enriched in functions related to cell differentiation, negative regulation of proliferation and cell type-specific metabolic pathways.
source: Moreover, these introns preferentially affected genes that were significantly enriched in functions related to cell differentiation, negative regulation of proliferation and cell type-specific metabolic pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Neoblast-specific intron retention may operate to ensure that a subset of early-transcribed differentiation genes is not active in neoblasts.
source: Therefore, altogether these data suggest that neoblast-specific IR may be operating to ensure that a subset of early-transcribed differentiation genes is not active in neoblasts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that X1-included introns disrupt reading frames and affect differentiation genes.

claim: Differentiation genes with detained introns might be selectively activated upon differentiation by splicing out the detained intron.
source: These genes might then be selectively activated upon differentiation by splicing out the 'detained' intron, similar to recent reports in mammalian ESCs (Boutz et al., 2015; Braunschweig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with mammalian ESC studies.

claim: Dugesia japonica has diverged from Schmidtea mediterranea approximately 85 million years ago.
source: To investigate whether the neoblast-differential AS program of S. mediterranea has been conserved during evolution, we mapped our validated set of AS exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) to a transcriptome assembly of the planarian species Dugesia japonica (Nishimura et al., 2015), which has diverged from S. mediterranea approximately 85 million years ago (Lazaro et al., 2011), similar to the estimated time for the human-mouse divergence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Lazaro et al., 2011.

claim: The divergence time between D. japonica and S. mediterranea is similar to the estimated time for the human-mouse divergence.
source: To investigate whether the neoblast-differential AS program of S. mediterranea has been conserved during evolution, we mapped our validated set of AS exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) to a transcriptome assembly of the planarian species Dugesia japonica (Nishimura et al., 2015), which has diverged from S. mediterranea approximately 85 million years ago (Lazaro et al., 2011), similar to the estimated time for the human-mouse divergence.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mammalian divergence times.

claim: 95.2% (20/21) of probed cassette exons were present and alternatively spliced in D. japonica.
source: Strikingly, 20/21 (95.2%) of the probed cassette exons were also present and alternatively spliced in D. japonica, and 16/20 (80%) of these showed conserved differential regulation between X1 and Xins fractions in the two species (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica.

claim: 80% (16/20) of alternatively spliced cassette exons showed conserved differential regulation between X1 and Xins fractions in S. mediterranea and D. japonica.
source: Strikingly, 20/21 (95.2%) of the probed cassette exons were also present and alternatively spliced in D. japonica, and 16/20 (80%) of these showed conserved differential regulation between X1 and Xins fractions in the two species (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica.

claim: Half (3/6) of the IR events that could be probed displayed conserved neoblast-differential regulation between S. mediterranea and D. japonica.
source: Moreover, half of the IR events that could be probed despite the lack of a reference genome sequence in D. japonica also displayed conserved neoblast-differential regulation (3/6; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica.

claim: The level of neoblast-differential conservation between planarian species is higher than that observed between ESC-differential exons in mammals.
source: This level of neoblast-differential conservation is even higher than that observed between ESC-differential exons in mammals (Han et al., 2013), and strongly argues for the functional relevance of this AS program in planarians.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with mammalian ESC studies.

claim: 15 orthologous gene groups have neoblast/ESC-differential exons in both planarian and humans.
source: We identified 15 orthologous gene groups with neoblast/ESC-differential exons in both planarian and humans (Figure 3—source data 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by orthology analysis between planarian and human genes.

claim: In ten orthologous groups, planarian and human stem cell regulated exons fall in similar regions of the protein.
source: Remarkably, in ten of these orthologous groups, planarian and human stem cell regulated exons fall in similar regions of the protein, and in at least four of them (add3, eml4, fmnl3 and ppfibp1) the intervening sequences are partly orthologous, despite extensive rearrangement of intron-exon structures (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment and intron position mapping analysis.

claim: In at least four orthologous groups (add3, eml4, fmnl3 and ppfibp1), the intervening sequences are partly orthologous between planarian and human.
source: Remarkably, in ten of these orthologous groups, planarian and human stem cell regulated exons fall in similar regions of the protein, and in at least four of them (add3, eml4, fmnl3 and ppfibp1) the intervening sequences are partly orthologous, despite extensive rearrangement of intron-exon structures (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Over 300 putative RNA binding proteins were identified in planarians based on homology searches and presence of RNA binding domains.
source: Based on homology searches and presence of RNA binding domains, we identified over 300 putative RNA binding proteins in planarians (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational annotation using InterProScan and BLAST.

claim: Smed-bruno-like (bruli), a member of the CELF family, showed the strongest differential expression enrichment in X1 fractions among the multiple probed AS factors.
source: Strikingly, a member of the CELF family (Smed-bruno-like, bruli) of AS regulators showed the strongest differential expression enrichment in X1 fractions among the multiple probed AS factors (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1), and had been previously reported to be needed for planarian stem cell self-renewal and regeneration (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq gene expression analysis.

claim: bruli had been previously reported to be needed for planarian stem cell self-renewal and regeneration.
source: Strikingly, a member of the CELF family (Smed-bruno-like, bruli) of AS regulators showed the strongest differential expression enrichment in X1 fractions among the multiple probed AS factors (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1), and had been previously reported to be needed for planarian stem cell self-renewal and regeneration (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Guo et al., 2006.

claim: bruli(RNAi) showed a dramatic phenotype with no regeneration.
source: As previously reported, bruli(RNAi) showed a dramatic phenotype with no regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays after RNAi treatment.

claim: ptbp(RNAi) group showed a similar phenotype to bruli(RNAi) with no regeneration.
source: A similar phenotype was also observed for the ptbp(RNAi) group.
evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays after RNAi treatment.

claim: Combined knockdown of the three other CELF factors enriched in Xins fractions induced elongation and movement defects but did not affect regeneration time dynamics.
source: Combined knockdown of the three other CELF factors, enriched in Xins fractions, induced elongation and movement defects, but did not seem to affect regeneration time dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays and phenotypic observation after RNAi treatment.

claim: A significant delay in regeneration was observed for the mbnl group knockdown.
source: Finally, a significant delay in regeneration was observed for the mbnl group.
evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays after RNAi treatment.

claim: bruli(RNAi) treatment induced dramatic changes in inclusion levels in X1 fractions towards the differentiated pattern.
source: Only bruli(RNAi) treatment induced dramatic changes in inclusion levels in X1 fractions compared to the control RNAi in the expected direction (i.e. towards the differentiated pattern; Figure 4C), suggesting that bruli may act as a positive regulator of the neoblast AS program.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis of AS events in FACS-sorted X1 cells after RNAi.

claim: bruli may act as a positive regulator of the neoblast AS program.
source: Only bruli(RNAi) treatment induced dramatic changes in inclusion levels in X1 fractions compared to the control RNAi in the expected direction (i.e. towards the differentiated pattern; Figure 4C), suggesting that bruli may act as a positive regulator of the neoblast AS program.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bruli knockdown shifts AS patterns toward differentiated patterns.

claim: Knockdown of the mbnl group showed the most widespread changes in the X1-differential AS program towards the neoblast pattern.
source: Knockdown of the mbnl group [a four-gene knockdown: Smed-mbnl-1;Smed-mbnl-like-1, -2, -3(RNAi), hereafter mbnl(RNAi)] (Figure 4—source data 3) showed the most widespread changes in the X1-differential AS program towards the neoblast pattern (Figure 4D), suggesting that MBNL proteins may act as negative regulators of the neoblast AS program.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of whole worms after RNAi treatment.

claim: MBNL proteins may act as negative regulators of the neoblast AS program.
source: Knockdown of the mbnl group [a four-gene knockdown: Smed-mbnl-1;Smed-mbnl-like-1, -2, -3(RNAi), hereafter mbnl(RNAi)] (Figure 4—source data 3) showed the most widespread changes in the X1-differential AS program towards the neoblast pattern (Figure 4D), suggesting that MBNL proteins may act as negative regulators of the neoblast AS program.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mbnl knockdown shifts AS patterns toward neoblast patterns.

claim: MBNL consensus motifs are the most significantly enriched in the downstream introns of X1-excluded cassette exons.
source: Remarkably, RNA sequence motif enrichment analyses using a library of RNAcompete-derived binding profiles for over 100 animal RBPs (Ray et al., 2013) showed that MBNL consensus motifs are also the most significantly enriched in the downstream introns of X1-excluded cassette exons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational motif enrichment analysis using RNAcompete data.

claim: Planarian MBNL proteins enhance X1-excluded exons via binding to their downstream introns.
source: This result is consistent with planarian MBNL proteins enhancing X1-excluded exons via binding to their downstream introns, as described for mammalian MBNL proteins (Han et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from motif enrichment data and comparison with mammalian MBNL function.

claim: Four potential mbnl orthologs were found in the planarian transcriptome.
source: We found four potential mbnl orthologs in the planarian transcriptome, comprising a canonical MBNL ortholog with two pairs of zinc finger domains (Smed-mbnl-1, hereafter mbnl-1), as well as three orthologs with only one pair (Smed-mbnl-like-1,2,3, hereafter mbnl-like-1,2,3) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and domain identification.

claim: All mbnl orthologs displayed expression enrichment in Xins fractions.
source: All mbnl orthologs displayed expression enrichment in Xins fractions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq gene expression analysis.

claim: mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern.
source: Whole mount in situ hybridizations showed that mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern, while mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue (Figure 5A; no expression was detected for mbnl-like-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue.
source: Whole mount in situ hybridizations showed that mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern, while mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue (Figure 5A; no expression was detected for mbnl-like-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: No expression was detected for mbnl-like-3 by in situ hybridization.
source: Whole mount in situ hybridizations showed that mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern, while mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue (Figure 5A; no expression was detected for mbnl-like-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Single-cell sequencing data revealed expression of mbnl-1, mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 in epidermis.
source: Analysis of recently published single-cell sequencing data further revealed expression of mbnl-1, mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 in epidermis, which is commonly lost in whole-mount in situ protocols, and confirmed the widespread expression of mbnl-1 (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell sequencing data.

claim: bruli was specifically expressed in neoblasts.
source: In contrast, as previously reported (Guo et al., 2006), bruli was specifically expressed in neoblasts, as shown both by in situ hybridization (Figure 5A) and single-cell sequencing data (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and single-cell sequencing data.

claim: The effects of bruli and mbnl knockdown on AS events are detectable 5 days after RNAi and are permanent for at least 30 days.
source: Importantly, while the regeneration phenotype was observed 22 days after the RNAi injection, effects on AS inclusion levels where observable as soon as five days after the initiation of the treatment, plateauing after day 10 post-injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course RT-PCR analysis after RNAi treatment.

claim: bruli knockdown induced strong inclusion level changes in X1 fractions towards the differentiated pattern (P = 1.4 × 10−19).
source: Consistent with our RT-PCR results (Figure 4C), bruli knockdown induced strong inclusion level changes in X1 fractions towards the differentiated pattern (Figure 6A; P = 1.4 × 10−19, binomial test).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-sorted X1 cells after RNAi treatment.

claim: mbnl knockdown induced changes in the opposite direction in Xins fractions (P = 2.1 × 10−11).
source: On the other hand, mbnl knockdown induced changes in the opposite direction in Xins fractions (Figure 6B; P = 2.1 × 10−11, binomial test).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-sorted Xins cells after RNAi treatment.

claim: Changes in inclusion levels obtained by RNA-seq analyses were independently validated by RT-PCR assays (19/19 changes, 100%; R2 = 0.87).
source: These changes in inclusion levels obtained by RNA-seq analyses were independently validated by RT-PCR assays (19/19 changes, 100%; R2 = 0.87, n = 225; Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation of RNA-Seq results.

claim: 37.9% (33/87) of mbnl-regulated AS events were also affected by bruli knockdown in the opposite direction (P = 2.2 × 10−7).
source: Remarkably, 33/87 (37.9%) mbnl-regulated AS events (14 cassette exons, 11 microexons, and 8 retained introns) were also affected by bruli knockdown in the opposite direction (Figure 6D; P = 2.2 × 10−7, binomial test; corresponding to 33/141 (23.4%) bruli-regulated AS events).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis comparing bruli and mbnl knockdown effects.

claim: 33.6% (37/110) of X1-retained introns showed decreased retention upon bruli knockdown (ΔPSI ≥ 15).
source: Of note, 37/110 (33.6%) of X1-retained introns showed decreased retention upon bruli knockdown (ΔPSI ≥ 15), suggesting that BRULI regulates coordinated IR events in planarian stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of intron retention after bruli knockdown.

claim: BRULI regulates coordinated IR events in planarian stem cells.
source: Of note, 37/110 (33.6%) of X1-retained introns showed decreased retention upon bruli knockdown (ΔPSI ≥ 15), suggesting that BRULI regulates coordinated IR events in planarian stem cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that many X1-retained introns are affected by bruli knockdown.

claim: mbnl knockdown affected 37% (20/54) of Xins-enriched microexons.
source: On the other hand, mbnl knockdown affected a large fraction of Xins-enriched microexons (20/54, 37%).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of microexons after mbnl knockdown.

claim: The binding specificities of planarian and mammalian MBNL and CELF homologs strongly correlated.
source: Moreover, the binding specificities of the planarian and mammalian homologs strongly correlated (Figure 6E) and highly significantly overlapped (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D; p<5.5 × 10−89 for all pairwise homolog comparisons, hypergeometric test) across all measured 7-mers in RNAcompete assays.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAcompete assays comparing planarian and mammalian proteins.

claim: The binding specificities of planarian and mammalian MBNL and CELF homologs highly significantly overlapped (p<5.5 × 10−89).
source: Moreover, the binding specificities of the planarian and mammalian homologs strongly correlated (Figure 6E) and highly significantly overlapped (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D; p<5.5 × 10−89 for all pairwise homolog comparisons, hypergeometric test) across all measured 7-mers in RNAcompete assays.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAcompete data.

claim: Planarian MBNL and CELF factors and mammalian homologs have conserved binding specificities.
source: Thus, the planarian MBNL and CELF factors and its mammalian homologs have conserved binding specificities.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAcompete assays showing conserved binding motifs.

claim: BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in the downstream introns of exons downregulated upon the respective KD.
source: Both BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in the downstream introns of exons downregulated upon the respective KD, whereas MBNL-1 motifs were also significantly enriched in exonic sequences of exons upregulated upon mbnl KD (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of regulated exons.

claim: MBNL-1 motifs were significantly enriched in exonic sequences of exons upregulated upon mbnl KD.
source: Both BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in the downstream introns of exons downregulated upon the respective KD, whereas MBNL-1 motifs were also significantly enriched in exonic sequences of exons upregulated upon mbnl KD (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of regulated exons.

claim: The locations of BRULI and MBNL binding motifs are consistent with enhancing or repressive functions from RNA regulatory maps described for these factors in mammals.
source: These locations are consistent with the enhancing or repressive functions, respectively, from RNA regulatory maps described for these factors in mammals (Han et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012), and strongly suggest a direct regulatory role in AS regulation in planarians.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with mammalian RNA regulatory maps.

claim: BRULI and MBNL have a direct regulatory role in AS regulation in planarians.
source: These locations are consistent with the enhancing or repressive functions, respectively, from RNA regulatory maps described for these factors in mammals (Han et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012), and strongly suggest a direct regulatory role in AS regulation in planarians.
evidence: This claim is inferred from motif enrichment data and comparison with mammalian regulatory mechanisms.

claim: bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype.
source: It was previously described that bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype (Guo et al., 2006). Consistently, we observed a strong downregulation of neoblast markers after bruli knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and RNA-Seq analysis of neoblast markers.

claim: Neoblast markers were strongly downregulated after bruli knockdown.
source: It was previously described that bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype (Guo et al., 2006). Consistently, we observed a strong downregulation of neoblast markers after bruli knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of marker gene expression.

claim: Neoblast markers were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
source: It was previously described that bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype (Guo et al., 2006). Consistently, we observed a strong downregulation of neoblast markers after bruli knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of marker gene expression.

claim: prog-1 and prog-2-1 are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors.
source: Strikingly, the progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2-1, which are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), changed their expression levels in opposing directions upon bruli/mbnl knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: bruli knockdown induced loss of prog-1 and prog-2-1 markers.
source: Strikingly, the progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2-1, which are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), changed their expression levels in opposing directions upon bruli/mbnl knockdown. More precisely, bruli knockdown induced loss of these markers, whereas mbnl knockdown led to an increase in their expression (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq and qPCR analysis of marker gene expression.

claim: mbnl knockdown led to an increase in prog-1 and prog-2-1 expression.
source: Strikingly, the progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2-1, which are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), changed their expression levels in opposing directions upon bruli/mbnl knockdown. More precisely, bruli knockdown induced loss of these markers, whereas mbnl knockdown led to an increase in their expression (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq and qPCR analysis of marker gene expression.

claim: The concomitant decrease and increase in the expression of multiple progeny markers for bruli and mbnl knockdown is likely due to the loss and accumulation of progenitors, respectively.
source: This concomitant decrease and increase in the expression of multiple progeny markers for bruli and mbnl knockdown, respectively, is likely due to the loss and accumulation of progenitors, respectively, rather than to specific changes in the expression levels of these markers in an invariant pool of progenitor cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of opposing changes in progeny marker expression.

claim: Cluster 1 genes were highly significantly decreased upon bruli knockdown (p<5.6 × 10−56).
source: Consistent with a prominent neoblast loss (Guo et al., 2006), Cluster 1 genes were highly significantly decreased upon bruli knockdown (Figure 7D ; p<5.6 × 10−56 for the three time points, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and statistical testing of gene expression changes.

claim: mbnl knockdown impacted predominantly Cluster six genes (p<0.01).
source: In contrast, mbnl knockdown impacted predominantly Cluster six genes (Figure 7D ; p<0.01 for the three time points, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and statistical testing of gene expression changes.

claim: The opposed effects of bruli and mbnl were reflected in the gene functions altered upon knockdown.
source: These opposed effects of bruli and mbnl were also reflected in the gene functions altered upon knockdown, with stem cell function-related terms enriched in bruli(RNAi) decreased genes, compared to differentiated tissue function associated terms for mbnl(RNAi) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Principal Component Analysis showed that the first PC sharply separated bruli samples together with Smed-H2B(RNAi) from mbnl samples together with Smedwi-2(RNAi).
source: In addition, a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) showed that the first PC sharply separated bruli samples together with Smed-H2B(RNAi)(which affects neoblast self-maintenance [Solana et al., 2012]) from mbnl samples together with Smedwi-2(RNAi)(which impairs neoblast differentiation [Reddien et al., 2005]) (Figure 7G), further showing their opposing effects in stem cell properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by Principal Component Analysis of transcriptomic data.

claim: Both CELF and MBNL factors are required for regeneration in planarians in vivo.
source: Taken together our results show that both CELF and MBNL factors are required for regeneration in planarians in vivo, and that they act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing regeneration defects.

claim: CELF and MBNL factors act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
source: Taken together our results show that both CELF and MBNL factors are required for regeneration in planarians in vivo, and that they act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the opposing effects of bruli and mbnl knockdown on AS patterns and cellular phenotypes.

claim: MBNL proteins are major direct negative regulators of mammalian ESC-differential AS.
source: Moreover, MBNL proteins have been shown to be major direct negative regulators of mammalian ESC-differential AS (Han et al., 2013; Venables et al., 2013), similarly to what we describe here for planarian neoblast AS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only seven orthologous gene groups have MBNL-regulated, non-homologous, exons in both planarians and humans.
source: While MBNL targets are largely not shared between planarians and humans (only seven orthologous gene groups have MBNL-regulated, non-homologous, exons in both species), the upstream role of MBNL proteins as repressors of stem cell-differential AS appears equivalent in both species.
evidence: This claim is supported by orthology analysis of MBNL-regulated exons.

claim: The upstream role of MBNL proteins as repressors of stem cell-differential AS appears equivalent in planarians and humans.
source: While MBNL targets are largely not shared between planarians and humans (only seven orthologous gene groups have MBNL-regulated, non-homologous, exons in both species), the upstream role of MBNL proteins as repressors of stem cell-differential AS appears equivalent in both species.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MBNL proteins repress stem cell AS in both species despite different targets.

claim: Direct negative regulation of stem cell transcriptomes by MBNL proteins, and perhaps positively by CELF factors, is a deeply conserved ancestral feature of animal stem cells.
source: This suggests that direct negative regulation of stem cell transcriptomes by MBNL proteins, and perhaps positively by CELF factors, is a deeply conserved ancestral feature of animal stem cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the conservation of MBNL and CELF function across distant species.

claim: Sponges differentially express a CELF homolog in their stem cells and an MBNL homolog in differentiated cells.
source: Indeed, a recent study has shown that sponges – the most basal metazoan lineage –also differentially express a CELF homolog in their stem cells and an MBNL homolog in differentiated cells (Alié et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Alié et al., 2015.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, a Bruno homolog (aret) is only highly expressed in the early pluripotent embryo stages (from 0 to 4 hr post fertilization) during development.
source: For instance, in Drosophila melanogaster a Bruno homolog (aret) is only highly expressed in the early pluripotent embryo stages (from 0 to 4 hr post fertilization) during development, while the embryonic expression of the single Mbnl ortholog (mbl) gradually increases from 6 hr post fertilization (Graveley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Graveley et al., 2011.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the embryonic expression of the single Mbnl ortholog (mbl) gradually increases from 6 hr post fertilization.
source: For instance, in Drosophila melanogaster a Bruno homolog (aret) is only highly expressed in the early pluripotent embryo stages (from 0 to 4 hr post fertilization) during development, while the embryonic expression of the single Mbnl ortholog (mbl) gradually increases from 6 hr post fertilization (Graveley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Graveley et al., 2011.

claim: The binding specificities of BRULI and MBNL proteins are very similar to those of their human counterparts.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that not only the antagonistic expression but also the binding specificities of BRULI and MBNL proteins are very similar to those of their human counterparts, an observation that is in line with the high level of conservation of binding specificities and positional regulatory codes described for several other RBPs (Brooks et al., 2011; Irimia et al., 2011; Lareau and Brenner, 2015; Ray et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012; Loria et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAcompete assays and citations to previous work on RBP conservation.

claim: The conservation of CELF and MBNL antagonism contrasts with the apparent high turnaround of stem cell regulation at the transcription factor level.
source: In summary, we have unveiled an ancient post-transcriptional antagonistic regulatory switch formed by CELF and MBNL factors that is associated with pluripotency in multiple animal systems. This evolutionary conservation contrasts with the apparent high turnaround of stem cell regulation at the transcription factor level, in which the core set of TFs that regulate mammalian ESCs is likely a lineage-specific innovation (Fernandez-Tresguerres et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with transcription factor conservation and citation to previous work.

claim: The core set of transcription factors that regulate mammalian ESCs is likely a lineage-specific innovation.
source: In summary, we have unveiled an ancient post-transcriptional antagonistic regulatory switch formed by CELF and MBNL factors that is associated with pluripotency in multiple animal systems. This evolutionary conservation contrasts with the apparent high turnaround of stem cell regulation at the transcription factor level, in which the core set of TFs that regulate mammalian ESCs is likely a lineage-specific innovation (Fernandez-Tresguerres et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Fernandez-Tresguerres et al., 2010.

claim: Single neoblasts transplanted into lethally irradiated hosts can rescue lethality, restore tissue turnover, generate all cell types of the adult planarian and completely transform the genotype and phenotype of the host into that of the donor.
source: Illustrating their pluripotency, single neoblasts transplanted into lethally irradiated hosts can rescue this lethality, restore tissue turnover, generate all cell types of the adult planarian and completely transform the genotype and phenotype of the host into that of the donor (Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Wagner et al., 2011.

claim: The neoblast pool is highly heterogeneous, including multiple lineage-committed precursors.
source: However, recent analyses at single-cell resolution showed that the neoblast pool is highly heterogeneous, also including multiple lineage-committed precursors (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014.

claim: Hundreds of genes are differentially enriched in both planarian and mammalian stem cells compared to all differentiated cell types despite 500 million years of independent evolution.
source: Initial transcriptomic analyses of planarian neoblasts have revealed hundreds of genes that are differentially enriched in both planarian and mammalian stem cells compared to all differentiated cell types despite 500 million years of independent evolution (Labbé et al., 2012; Onal et al., 2012; Reddien et al., 2005; Resch et al., 2012; Rouhana et al., 2010; Solana et al., 2012), suggesting the existence of universal regulatory features across animal pluripotent cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous transcriptomic studies.

claim: The conservation of stem cell genes suggests the existence of universal regulatory features across animal pluripotent cells.
source: Initial transcriptomic analyses of planarian neoblasts have revealed hundreds of genes that are differentially enriched in both planarian and mammalian stem cells compared to all differentiated cell types despite 500 million years of independent evolution (Labbé et al., 2012; Onal et al., 2012; Reddien et al., 2005; Resch et al., 2012; Rouhana et al., 2010; Solana et al., 2012), suggesting the existence of universal regulatory features across animal pluripotent cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of conserved gene expression patterns.

claim: The major transcriptional regulators of mammalian stem cells are not conserved beyond the vertebrate lineage.
source: However, this conservation does not include the major transcriptional regulators of mammalian stem cells. In ESCs, pluripotency is maintained by a core set of transcription factors that include OCT4, NANOG and SOX2, but these factors and their interactions are largely not conserved beyond the vertebrate lineage (Fernandez-Tresguerres et al., 2010; Gold et al., 2014; Onal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on transcription factor conservation.

claim: No homolog of NANOG has been described to date in any invertebrate species.
source: For instance, no homolog of NANOG has been described to date in any invertebrate species, despite extensive search (Scerbo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Scerbo et al., 2014.

claim: MBNL proteins are lowly expressed in mammalian ESCs but show higher levels of expression in all profiled differentiated samples.
source: For example, members of the MBNL family of RBPs are lowly expressed in mammalian ESCs, but show higher levels of expression in all profiled differentiated samples – ranging from transformed cell lines (e.g. HeLa, 293T, etc.) to highly histologically and functionally diverse adult tissue types (including multiple brain regions, muscle, liver, kidney, testis, etc.) – where they repress a program of alternative exons that are characteristic of ESCs (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Han et al., 2013.

claim: MBNL proteins repress a program of alternative exons that are characteristic of ESCs in differentiated cells.
source: For example, members of the MBNL family of RBPs are lowly expressed in mammalian ESCs, but show higher levels of expression in all profiled differentiated samples – ranging from transformed cell lines (e.g. HeLa, 293T, etc.) to highly histologically and functionally diverse adult tissue types (including multiple brain regions, muscle, liver, kidney, testis, etc.) – where they repress a program of alternative exons that are characteristic of ESCs (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Han et al., 2013.

claim: Knockdown of MBNL in differentiated cultured cells induces ESC-like AS patterns and enhances somatic cell reprogramming.
source: Knockdown of MBNL in differentiated cultured cells thus induces ESC-like AS patterns and this is sufficient to enhance somatic cell reprogramming (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Han et al., 2013.

claim: MBNL-regulated AS of the transcription factor FOXP1 in mouse and human embryonic stem cells changes its DNA-binding properties.
source: For instance, MBNL-regulated AS of the transcription factor FOXP1 in mouse and human embryonic stem cells changes its DNA-binding properties, so that its stem cell specific isoform (FOXP1-ES) promotes transcription of pluripotency genes and represses differentiation genes, while its canonical isoform activates genes involved in differentiation (Gabut et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Gabut et al., 2011.

claim: FOXP1-ES is repressed by MBNL upon differentiation by direct binding to intronic regions in the pre-mRNA.
source: Consistently, FOXP1-ES is repressed by MBNL upon differentiation by direct binding to intronic regions in the pre-mRNA (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Han et al., 2013.

claim: Members of the CELF RBP family regulate AS in an antagonistic manner to that of MBNL factors in mammals.
source: Intriguingly, members of another RBP family, CELF, have been shown to regulate AS in an antagonistic manner to that of MBNL factors in mammals.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CELF and MBNL antagonism.

claim: During heart development, CELF factors promote embryonic AS patterns, which are later replaced by adult heart AS patterns promoted by MBNL proteins.
source: For example, during heart development, CELF factors promote embryonic AS patterns, which are later replaced by adult heart AS patterns promoted by MBNL proteins (Kalsotra et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Kalsotra et al., 2008.

claim: Multiple exons have been shown to antagonistically respond to CELF and MBNL factors in a variety of mammalian differentiation, disease and cell culture systems.
source: Multiple exons have been shown to antagonistically respond to CELF and MBNL factors in a variety of mammalian differentiation, disease and cell culture systems (Dasgupta and Ladd, 2012; Kalsotra et al., 2008; Lee and Cooper, 2009; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: CELF factors have not been linked to regulation of AS in stem cells prior to this study.
source: CELF factors, however, have not been linked so far to regulation of AS in stem cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior reports linking CELF to stem cell AS regulation.

claim: ~80% of the cells in adult planarians are differentiated.
source: This latter correlation is expected since ~80% of the cells in adult planarians are differentiated (Baguñà and Romero, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Baguñà and Romero, 1981.
